{"id": "3:79/q01", "question": "What does mā kāna li-bashar deny?", "turns_on": "Whether the formula denies possibility, propriety, or only legal permission.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q01/p1", "position": "Unfitting or unauthorized act", "reasons": "BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516: The phrase means that it is not appropriate for a human to receive scripture, judgment, and prophethood and then tell people to worship him. | mentions 24:16 IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 citing أبو بكر: Abū Bakr illustrates this absolute negative form by saying that it was not fitting for Ibn Abī Quḥāfa to pray before the Messenger. TABRISI, d. 548: ما كان لبشر means that it is unfitting for a human being to do this, as in the cited examples. | mentions 4:92, 24:16 IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597: Kāna can mean “ought” or “should,” expressing that something is not proper. | mentions 4:92, 42:51, 24:16 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671: Mā kāna here means it is not fitting or proper, as in the cited verses. | mentions 4:92, 19:35, 24:16 SAMIN-DURR, d. 756: The second type denies propriety rather than occurrence, as in Abu Bakr’s statement that it was not fitting for Ibn Abi Quhafa to lead prayer before the Messenger; context distinguishes the types. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270: The phrase mā kāna can mean that such conduct is not valid, not appropriate, or not permitted."}, {"id": "3:79/q01/p2", "position": "Categorical impossibility", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542: The wording is a complete negation whose force depends on context; unlike logical impossibilities, this verse categorically excludes God giving prophethood to liars and pretenders. RAZI-FULL, d. 606: The wording instead negates the claim, as 19:35 negates God taking a son and 3:161 negates a prophet committing fraud rather than merely forbidding those acts. | mentions 19:35, 3:161 SAMIN-DURR, d. 756: Here the denial is complete: God does not grant scripture, judgment, and prophecy to someone who says such a blasphemous thing; 27:60 and 3:145 illustrate the form. | mentions 27:60, 3:145 BIQAI-FULL, d. 885: The phrase ma kāna means such a thing was neither valid nor conceivable in any way. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393: The entitlement construction is the source of the emphatic lam of denial, as in the verse saying God would not punish them; that pattern emphatically disowns the act as incompatible with the subject's nature. | mentions 8:33"}, {"id": "3:79/q01/p3", "position": "Unfitting act", "reasons": "THALABI: Unfitting act (as recorded by THALABI). DAMGHANI: Unfitting act (as recorded by DAMGHANI)."}, {"id": "3:79/q01/p4", "position": "Context determines force of denial", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542: He contrasts this with other ‘it was not for’ constructions, including one expressing impossibility and one about bringing forth a tree. | mentions 3:145, 16:60 SAMIN-DURR, d. 756: The Arabic formula ما كان لزيد أن يفعل has two contextual senses: denial that the act can or does occur, or rejection that it is appropriate."}, {"id": "3:79/q01/p5", "position": "Kāna denotes existence or an attribute", "reasons": "IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 citing علي بن عبيد الله: Kāna is a past-tense verb whose basic sense is to occur or exist; it is complete without a predicate for existence and defective with a predicate for an attribute. IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 citing علي بن عبيد الله: When kāna describes an attribute, it is defective and requires a predicate."}, {"id": "3:79/q01/p6", "position": "Impermissible act", "reasons": "TABRISI, d. 548: Another interpretation is that such conduct is impermissible and unlawful for a human being."}, {"id": "3:79/q01/p7", "position": "Exoneration rather than prohibition", "reasons": "TABRISI, d. 548: The statement exonerates the Prophet from such a claim; it is not phrased as a prohibition addressed to him."}]}
{"id": "3:79/q02", "question": "How is the opening construction parsed?", "turns_on": "The notes give different senses, referents, readings, or explanations for this wording.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q02/p1", "position": "Entitlement construction with an-clause", "reasons": "ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745: The construction mā kāna li-basharin negates the predicate; negation can express rational impossibility or an impossibility appropriate to context, and this verse uses the first kind. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270: The preposed lām phrase is the predicate of kāna and the clause with an is its subject; an implied conjunction is needed for sound meaning, since many humans received scripture and prophethood. TABATABAI, d. 1402: The lām in ma kāna li-bashar denotes ownership or entitlement: the human has no right to do this, as in the cited Qur'anic formulations. | mentions 24:16, 3:161 TABATABAI, d. 1402: The phrase about God granting scripture, judgment, and prophethood is the subject of kāna and prepares for the following clause; its inclusion signals that divine grant itself is central."}, {"id": "3:79/q02/p2", "position": "Lam with an-clause", "reasons": "THALABI: Lam with an-clause (as recorded by THALABI)."}, {"id": "3:79/q02/p3", "position": "Adjectival clause and displaced an", "reasons": "WAHIDI-BASIT: Adjectival clause and displaced an (as recorded by WAHIDI-BASIT)."}, {"id": "3:79/q02/p4", "position": "Coordination semantically required", "reasons": "SAMIN-DURR, d. 756: Some coordinated complements are semantically obligatory, just like certain circumstantial and object phrases; this coordination is one such case."}]}
{"id": "3:79/q03", "question": "What does bashar mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q03/p1", "position": "Human generic collective", "reasons": "TAB-FULL: Human generic collective (as recorded by TAB-FULL). THALABI: Human generic collective (as recorded by THALABI). JISHUMI: Human generic collective (as recorded by JISHUMI). BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516: Bashar denotes all human beings and has no singular form from the same word; like qawm and jaysh it may refer to one person or a group. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542: Mā kāna li-bashar means ‘for anyone’; bashar is a collective noun usable for one or many and has no singular form of its own. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Bashar is synonymous with insan and can denote either one human being or a group."}]}
{"id": "3:79/q04", "question": "Who is the human in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the occasion and surrounding Christian polemic identify Jesus, Muhammad, or any endowed human.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q04/p1", "position": "Jesus", "reasons": "THALABI: Jesus (as recorded by THALABI). IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 citing الضحاك، مقاتل: Another view identifies the human as Jesus and the Book as the Gospel. RAZI-FULL, d. 606: Razi says the verse denies that a human granted scripture, judgment, and prophethood would make this claim; it does not merely prohibit speech already forbidden to everyone, which would not refute the charge against Jesus. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710: The verse denies that a human granted scripture, judgment, and prophethood could call people to worship him instead of God; this rebuts belief in Jesus's worship. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 citing النقاش وغيره: Al-Naqqāsh and others take the reference to be Jesus and read the verse as a rebuttal of Christians who claimed he was divine and that he commanded his own worship. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885: Bashar covers any human at all, including Jesus, Ezra, and others. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Tabatabai says the verses about no human recipient of scripture claiming worship fit Jesus more readily than Muhammad. | mentions 3:79 TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing تفسير القمي: The Qummī commentary says Jesus did not tell people to worship him; he called them rabbāniyyūn, meaning learned scholars. TABATABAI, d. 1402: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads the report's denial that Jesus claimed to create people as an argument that he could not have commanded them to worship him. TABATABAI, d. 1402: He says other reported occasions of revelation appear to be theoretical inferences, while several causes may coincide in the revelation of one verse. ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412: Asad identifies Jesus as the obvious referent and explains the sentence as saying that God grants a human revelation, judgment, and prophethood, after which he could not demand worship."}, {"id": "3:79/q04/p2", "position": "Muhammad", "reasons": "THALABI: Muhammad (as recorded by THALABI). WAHIDI-BASIT: Muhammad (as recorded by WAHIDI-BASIT). IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 citing ابن عباس والربيع وابن جريج وجماعة من المفسرين: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Rabīʿ, Ibn Jurayj, and other exegetes say the verse refers instead to Muḥammad. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 citing ابن عباس، عطاء: One view identifies the human addressed as Muhammad and the Book as the Quran. TABATABAI, d. 1402 citing بعض المفسرين: Some exegetes identify the verses with Muhammad, citing a report that Abu Rafi' al-Qurazi and a Christian from Najran asked whether he wanted them to worship him; they read the closing phrase as Islam brought by Muhammad."}, {"id": "3:79/q04/p3", "position": "Jesus son of Mary", "reasons": "MUQATIL: Jesus son of Mary (as recorded by MUQATIL)."}, {"id": "3:79/q04/p4", "position": "Muhammad as inferred application", "reasons": "TABATABAI, d. 1402: He suggests Ibn Abbas may have inferred and applied the verses about Muhammad, since the Qur'an often presents such statements as questions, answers, or narrated rebuttals. | mentions 3:79"}]}

{"id": "3:79/q06", "question": "What does al-ḥukm mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ḥukm denotes understanding, judgmental authority, or the Sunnah.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q06/p1", "position": "Knowledge or wisdom", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542: Al-kitāb is a generic noun, and al-ḥukm means wisdom, as in the Prophetic saying that poetry contains wisdom. TABRISI, d. 548: The granted book, wisdom, and prophethood are glossed as knowledge and a message to creation. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 citing قتادة: Al-hukm means jurisprudence and knowledge, according to Qatada and others. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745: Some interpret al-ḥukm as wisdom, with the saying that poetry contains wisdom offered as a parallel. BURSEVI, d. 1127: Hukm means understanding and knowledge, including wisdom as perfected knowledge and action; scholars of language and exegesis agree it means knowledge. | mentions 19:12 ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270: Here ḥukm means wisdom, as explained earlier. ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 citing Zamakhshari: Zamakhshari treats hukm, judgment or sound judgment, as synonymous here with hikmah, wisdom. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Hukm lexically means deciding, governing, restraining, or preventing; philosophically it is an affirmative or negative relation between ideas or states and its apprehension, and it is classified by knowledge source and field. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR citing İbn Atıyye: Ibn Atiyya explains hukm here as wisdom. | mentions 2:269 KURANYOLU-TEFSIR citing Muhammed Esed: Muhammad Asad renders hukm as sound judgment. STUDYQURAN: Ḥukm, translated as judgment, can also mean rule."}, {"id": "3:79/q06/p2", "position": "Adjudication or ruling", "reasons": "WAHIDI-BASIT: Adjudication or ruling (as recorded by WAHIDI-BASIT). BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516: Al-ḥukm is glossed either as understanding and knowledge or as the authority to enact God's judgment; prophethood is the prophets' exalted rank. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671: Al-kitāb means the Qur'an; al-ḥukm means knowledge and understanding, or alternatively legal judgments. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745: Al-kitāb is a generic noun; al-ḥukm is best understood as adjudication and judgment among people, following knowledge and preceding the higher rank of prophecy. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745: The apparent meaning is judgment and decision among people; the verse progresses from knowledge, to authority to judge, to the highest rank of prophethood. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885: Al-ḥukm is wisdom that equips one to judge: knowledge supported by action and action perfected by knowledge; its root denotes soundly putting each thing in its proper place. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: The Qur'an uses hukm of God for absolute will, sovereignty, and authority to decide, and of prophets or people for settling legal disputes. | mentions 6:57, 6:62, 12:40, 12:67, 28:70, 28:88, 4:58"}, {"id": "3:79/q06/p3", "position": "Knowledge or understanding", "reasons": "IBNABIHATIM: Knowledge or understanding (as recorded by IBNABIHATIM). IBNABIHATIM: Knowledge or understanding (as recorded by IBNABIHATIM). THALABI: Knowledge or understanding (as recorded by THALABI). WAHIDI-BASIT: Knowledge or understanding (as recorded by WAHIDI-BASIT)."}, {"id": "3:79/q06/p4", "position": "Wisdom identified with Sunna", "reasons": "KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538: Here الحكم means wisdom, identified with the Sunnah. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710: Al-ḥukm is glossed as wisdom, meaning either the Sunna or the ability to judge decisively."}, {"id": "3:79/q06/p5", "position": "Revelation, understanding, and prophecy", "reasons": "TAB-FULL: Revelation, understanding, and prophecy (as recorded by TAB-FULL)."}]}
{"id": "3:79/q07", "question": "Why are Book, judgment, and prophethood ordered this way?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q07/p1", "position": "Revelation, understanding, and mission", "reasons": "BURSEVI, d. 1127: The sequence is book revelation, the prophet’s grasp of its meaning and secrets, then his communication of that understanding to people as prophethood."}]}

QIRAAT-ER: The hamzated nubūʾa derives from n-b-ʾ, informing, rather than n-b-w, elevation, making the etymological fork phonologically explicit."}, {"id": "3:79/q09/p2", "position": "Nabi without hamza", "reasons": "JISHUMI: Nabi without hamza (as recorded by JISHUMI). {"id": "3:79/q10", "question": "How is thumma yaqūla read and parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether yaqūla remains governed by an or begins an independent sentence.", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q10/p1", "position": "Subjunctive coordinated", "reasons": "SIBAWAYH: Subjunctive coordinated (as recorded by SIBAWAYH). SIBAWAYH: Subjunctive coordinated (as recorded by SIBAWAYH). SIBAWAYH: Subjunctive coordinated (as recorded by SIBAWAYH). AKHFASH: Subjunctive coordinated (as recorded by AKHFASH). ZAJJAJ: Subjunctive coordinated (as recorded by ZAJJAJ). NAHHAS: Subjunctive coordinated (as recorded by NAHHAS). RAZI-FULL, d. 606: The common reading puts the verb after thumma in the subjunctive, indicating that prophethood and telling people to worship the prophet cannot coexist; it is governed by an implied an and coordinated with what came before. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671: Thumma yaqul is coordinated with the granting of scripture, judgment, and prophethood: a prophet cannot receive prophethood and then tell people to worship him instead of God. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710: The clause then he says is syntactically coordinated with God granting the person these gifts. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 citing الجمهور: The common reading has يقول in the accusative, coordinated to يؤتيه. Sībawayh, al-Akhfash, al-Zajjāj, and al-Naḥḥās coordinate ثم يقول with أن يؤتيه; al-Naḥḥās calls the accusative stronger."}, {"id": "3:79/q10/p2", "position": "Indicative detached restart", "reasons": "RAZI-FULL, d. 606 citing أبو عمرو: Abu Amr's reported indicative reading begins a new sentence. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745: Most readers use the subjunctive yaqūla, coordinated with yuʾtiyahu; Shibl from Ibn Kathīr and Maḥbūb from Abū ʿAmr use the indicative, with an implied huwa and a syntactic break. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 citing أبو عمرو: Abu Amr likewise has a nominative يقول in Mahbub’s transmission, parsed as a detached restart; the author questions how the sentence can then be complete."}, {"id": "3:79/q10/p3", "position": "Subjunctive or indicative", "reasons": "THALABI: Subjunctive or indicative (as recorded by THALABI). JISHUMI: Subjunctive or indicative (as recorded by JISHUMI)."}, {"id": "3:79/q10/p4", "position": "Indicative restart", "reasons": "NAHHAS: Indicative restart (as recorded by NAHHAS)."}]}
{"id": "3:79/q11", "question": "What does thumma contribute?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:79/q11/p1", "position": "Delay magnifies the offense", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542: Thumma heightens the gravity of the offense: the person would say this after a delay following such divine favor. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 citing قوم: One view reserves ʿibād for God’s servants and uses ʿabīd or ʿabdā for human slaves; another restricts ʿabdā to descendants of slaves as an emphatic form. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745: Most readers pronounce the possessive yāʾ in ʿibādan lī as quiescent, while ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar reads it with fatḥa. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 citing القاضي: Al-Qāḍī says ʿibād is the plural of ʿabd in the sense of worship; ʿabīd instead denotes servitude that can belong to someone other than God. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270: Wa-lākin kūnū rabbāniyyīn affirms what was denied: a prophet does not tell people to worship him but tells them to become learned, devout servants of God; the verb is coordinated in the subjunctive. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing ابن عطية: Ibn Atiyya notes that Arab Christians in al-Hira were called العباد, while عبيد appears in degrading phrases such as slaves of the stick and the line attributed here to Hamza b. al-Muttalib. STUDYQURAN: ʿIbād, singular ʿabd, means worshippers of something."}, {"id": "3:79/q12/p2", "position": "ʿIbād signals honor and obedience", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 citing امرؤ القيس: Imruʾ al-Qays’s line addresses people as ʿabīd, illustrating the term’s belittling force. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542: The Qur’anic phrase ‘not unjust to the slaves’ occurs in a context of compassion and their limited ability to defend themselves; ʿibād signals obedience, unlike the belittling ʿabīd. | mentions 41:46 IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542: He sees this lexical distinction as one of the remarkable ways Qur’anic eloquence follows sound Arabic usage. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542: Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s usage survey finds ʿibād in elevated contexts of obedience without belittlement, citing several Qur’anic examples. | mentions 2:207, 3:30, 21:26, 39:53, 5:118 ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 citing ابن عطية: Ibn ʿAṭiyya's lexical observation is that ʿibād occurs in contexts of elevation and obedience without contempt, as in several Qurʾanic descriptions. | mentions 2:207, 21:26, 39:53, 5:118 ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 citing ابن عطية: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says ʿabīd carries a belittling sense, citing Imruʾ al-Qays, Ḥamza, and the Qurʾanic phrase bẓallām lil-ʿabīd; he explains ʿibād as fitting the verse's sense of obedience. | mentions 39:53, 41:46 ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745: The claim that ʿibād is elevated and ʿabīd contemptuous is not a sound induction; ʿibād is simply the regular plural pattern for ʿabd, unlike ʿabīd. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 citing ابن عطية: Ibn Atiyya’s usage survey says عباد connotes elevation and obedience without contempt, citing 2:207, 21:26, 39:53, and 5:118; that positive sense explains its use in 39:53. | mentions 2:207, 21:26, 39:53, 5:118 SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 citing الشيخ: Al-Shaykh says عبيد and عباد have the same meaning and argues that the contempt in Imru al-Qays’s line and Hamza’s remark comes from context, not the word. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756: The author says al-Shaykh’s dismissal of Ibn Atiyya’s usage survey is unfounded without a counterexample, and rejects assigning contempt only to context when the word itself is the better source. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756: The author rejects the claim that contempt in عبيد is supplied only by context, arguing that lexical wording takes precedence when either word or context could explain it. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing ابن عطية: Ibn Atiyya says عباد is a plural of عبد without derogation, whereas عبيد carries a sense of abasement or servitude. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 citing ابن عطية: Ibn Atiyya uses God's denial of injustice to the عبيد as a compassionate reassurance, and God's address to sinful servants as consolation through the obedient form العباد. | mentions 41:46, 39:53 KURANYOLU-TEFSIR citing İbn Atıyye: Ibn Atiyya finds that Qur'anic ibad occurs in contexts that honor the servant's will to obey, without connotations of pity or contempt."}, {"id": "3:79/q12/p3", "position": "ʿIbād and ʿabīd are semantically equivalent", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 citing بعض اللغويين: Some linguists treat the plurals ʿibād, ʿabīd, and ʿabdā as synonymous. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745: Abū Ḥayyān challenges Ibn ʿAṭiyya's generalization: ʿabīd is most properly a plural, while ʿabdā is a collective noun with a feminine-marked alif. KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538: Rabbānī is formed from Rabb with the suffix alif-nūn and describes someone strongly attached to God's religion and obedience. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 citing قوم: One etymology derives rabbānī from rabb: a person who knows what God taught, obeys Him, and teaches people what He commanded; the extra alif and nūn intensify the relation. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 citing سيبويه: Sibawayh derives rabbānī from the Lord: it describes one devoted to knowing and obeying God; the added alif and nūn intensify the quality, as in words for abundant hair or a long beard.
